items.summary: Assessments to this day have relied on a correct-looking output as proof of an invisible underlying state, but today it is becoming increasingly unreliable. This raises a more intriguing question: what were we really attempting to see in the first place?

items.title: When journalism leaks into art: Interview with musician-journalist Carl La’Frenais
items.summary: Two people are on an unknown terrace, lying with their hands behind their heads and gazing at the night sky, missing the stars because they are too immersed in their conversation and laughing at a joke. Carl La’Frenais listens as I describe this image that flowed into my mind when his song ‘Happy Place’ was played. He laughs and then shares the real story behind it, which unsurprisingly lacks a terrace, the night sky, and the joke, but has the comforting presence of two people watching the sea together. The Fort Kochi beach is where Carl used to go early in the mornings to let his mind float before a busy day as a journalist began. Every morning, he would see an old man cycle to the beach and watch the sea, much like Carl, in total silence. Once, Carl asked him about it, and he said it was his happy place. He used to come there with his wife, but she was no longer with him, and he wanted to relive those memories and remember her every single day. “He said the visit was like going back to his happy place,” Carl says, in a brief chat about his new extended play (EP), which contains ‘Happy Place’ and three other songs, all of which are tributes to his hometown, Fort Kochi.
